reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Colles Fracture Distal Radius: dinner fork deformity of wrist after slipping on ice and falling onto outstretched hand. 64F with osteopenia presenting with dorsally displaced, angulated extra-articular distal radius fracture with radial shortening on radiographs.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Colles Fracture Distal Radius.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Colles Fracture Distal Radius.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain wrist radiographs and urgently document skin integrity, distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, and motor function. Immobilize, provide appropriate analgesia, and arrange reduction/casting or orthopedic management according to alignment and stability; repeat neurovascular checks after any manipulation or splinting. Escalate immediately for an open fracture, worsening pain/tight swelling, pale or cool fingers, or new numbness/weakness.

teaching.one_liner: 64F with osteopenia, fell on ice onto an outstretched hand, now with a dinner-fork wrist deformity.
red_flags: Neurovascular status of the hand must be checked

must_ask.say: Can you describe exactly how you fell and landed on your hand?
Does your wrist look bent or deformed to you?

must_ask.objective: Screen for finger numbness or color change
must_ask.say: Can you feel and move all your fingers normally, and are they a normal color?
Have you been diagnosed with weak bones or taken bone density medication?

must_ask.objective: Explain the reduction and casting plan
must_ask.say: We will first check circulation and nerve function and review the X-rays. If reduction is needed, it is done with appropriate pain control, followed by immobilization and repeat circulation and nerve checks; we should also arrange bone-health follow-up.

history.answer: I slipped on an icy patch about an hour ago and fell forward onto my outstretched right hand, and now my wrist is in agony and looks crooked like a fork.
Only my right wrist hurts and looks deformed. My left wrist and all my other joints feel completely normal.
It started all of a sudden about an hour ago, right when I fell onto the ice.
I was walking out to the mailbox, slipped on black ice, and put my right palm out flat to catch myself as I went down hard.
It is a severe, deep, throbbing ache that jumps to sharp agony if it gets bumped. I would rate it an 8 out of 10.
Yes, right after I fell I looked down and saw a strange hump on the back of my wrist, resembling the curve of an upside-down dinner fork.
It swelled up rapidly within minutes of the fall, but it does not feel burning hot or look red.
My fingers feel stiff from the swelling, but I can feel my fingertips normally and they have not turned blue, pale, or numb.
No, I have never had morning stiffness in my wrists or fingers.
Any attempt to move the wrist or let it dangle makes the pain unbearable, while supporting it completely still with my other hand helps slightly.
I cannot move my wrist at all, and I cannot hold or grasp anything with my right hand right now.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
Yes, I felt and heard a distinct crunching snap in my wrist the moment my palm hit the ground.
No, I have never had an injury, swelling, or sudden pain attack in this wrist before.
No, I have not had any unusual fatigue, low-grade fevers, or unintentional weight loss.
No rashes on my face or body, no scaly patches, no mouth sores, no hair thinning, and no red or dry eyes.
No, I do not have morning back stiffness, heel tenderness, or swelling in my fingers or toes.
No recent diarrhea, painful urination, vaginal discharge, or sore throat.
I have not had any alcoholic drinks, large meat or shellfish meals, or water pills.
I have never received joint injections, had joint surgery, or had artificial joints placed, and I have never taken oral steroids.
I have been happily married to my husband for over thirty years, and neither of us has any other partners.
About two years ago my primary care doctor ordered a bone density scan that showed mild bone thinning, or osteopenia, in my hips and spine.
I have had high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol for several years, along with the osteopenia.
I had my gallbladder removed laparoscopically about fifteen years ago, but I have had no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I take Lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure, along with an over-the-counter calcium and vitamin D pill.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, latex, or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine at a dinner party, perhaps once or twice a month.
I am a retired high school librarian living at home with my husband, and I normally stay very active with daily brisk walks and gardening.
My mother had severe osteoporosis and broke her hip when she was seventy-two, but no one in my family has rheumatoid arthritis or gout.
I'm pretty sure I broke my wrist when I slipped and fell on the ice. I'm scared that I'll need surgery with pins or plates and won't be able to manage living on my own while it heals.
I'm hoping to get an X-ray right away, some pain relief, and have this put into a cast today.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert and oriented woman in acute discomfort, sitting upright and cradling her right forearm and wrist with her left hand.
Intact skin over the right wrist and forearm without lacerations, tenting, or open wounds; no rash or tophi on either hand.

Obvious dinner fork deformity with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal right radius, marked swelling and severe tenderness over the distal radius and radial styloid, and active and passive wrist motion severely restricted by pain.
Right radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ and symmetric with the left, and capillary refill is brisk at under two seconds in all five digits.
Intact light touch sensation across the median, ulnar, and radial nerve distributions in the right hand, including the volar index and small fingertips.
Intact thumb opposition, finger abduction, and interphalangeal flexion and extension in all digits, though active wrist motion and grip testing are deferred due to severe pain.
